publishedSummary: The cardiac cycle is a sequence of pressure changes; valves and sounds simply follow from them. Once the pressures are clear, the timing of filling, the isovolumetric phases and the origin of each sound stop needing to be memorised separately.

sections.narrative:
Cardiac valves have no muscle and are not opened or closed by any active mechanism; each is moved entirely by the pressure difference across it. Every event in the cycle therefore reduces to a comparison of two pressures, and the two isovolumetric phases are simply the intervals when neither comparison favours opening.

At the start of systole the ventricle begins to contract with both its inlet and its outlet valves shut. The atrioventricular valve has closed because ventricular pressure now exceeds atrial pressure; the semilunar valve remains shut because ventricular pressure is still below arterial pressure. With no exit, contraction raises pressure without moving blood — hence isovolumetric contraction. It ends only when ventricular pressure rises above the pressure in the artery beyond: during isovolumetric contraction, ventricular pressure must rise above approximately 80 mmHg on the left and 10 mmHg on the right before the semilunar valves open. That eightfold difference is the reason the left ventricle is so much thicker than the right, and it is the reason afterload is a far more powerful constraint on the left side.

The mirror-image phase follows ejection. As the ventricle relaxes, its pressure falls below arterial pressure and the semilunar valve shuts, but it is still above atrial pressure, so the atrioventricular valve has not yet opened. All valves are closed and ventricular volume is constant during isovolumetric relaxation. The ventricle is a sealed chamber whose walls are relaxing, so pressure falls steeply, and this fall is what eventually drops ventricular pressure below atrial pressure and opens the atrioventricular valve to begin filling.

The cycle has a fixed budget of time that shortens as rate rises. At 75 beats per minute, one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds; atrial systole occupies roughly 0.1 seconds and atrial diastole about 0.7 seconds. The atria are therefore at rest for most of every cycle, which suits their role as reservoirs that fill continuously from the great veins.

The placement of atrial contraction within the cycle is the point most often misplaced. Atrial systole occupies the final part of ventricular diastole and is therefore a late-diastolic event. It does not begin ventricular filling; it completes it. By the time the atria contract, the atrioventricular valves have been open for some time and the ventricle has already filled substantially.

The numbers make clear how much this final contribution matters. At rest, about 80% of ventricular filling occurs passively before atrial contraction, while atrial contraction contributes the remaining 20%. Most filling is therefore driven simply by the pressure difference between atrium and relaxing ventricle, and the atrial kick is a supplement. This is why a resting patient may lose organised atrial contraction — in atrial fibrillation, for instance — with little immediate change in cardiac output.

That tolerance narrows with exertion. The atrial contribution to ventricular filling increases during exercise, for a reason that follows directly from the timing above: as heart rate rises, diastole shortens far more than systole does, leaving less time for passive filling, so the brief, well-timed atrial contraction accounts for a growing share of the total. A patient who is comfortable at rest without atrial contraction may therefore become markedly limited on exertion.

The normal heart sounds are produced by valve closure and by the abrupt deceleration of blood that accompanies it — the first sound as the atrioventricular valves close at the start of systole, the second as the semilunar valves close at its end. Between and around them, flow through a normal heart is laminar and therefore silent.

A cardiac murmur is an abnormal sound produced by turbulent blood flow and heard during cardiac auscultation. Turbulence arises when flow ceases to be smooth: when blood is forced through an opening that is too narrow, when it passes backward through a valve that should be shut, when it crosses an abnormal communication between chambers, or when flow through a normal orifice becomes fast enough to break down laminar flow on its own.

This is why the timing of a murmur within the cycle is so informative. Knowing which valves are open and which are closed at each moment converts a sound into an anatomical hypothesis: a murmur occurring while the ventricle is ejecting must involve the valve it is ejecting through or an abnormal outlet, whereas one occurring while the ventricle is filling must involve the valve it is filling through or an incompetent outlet valve. The murmur is not a separate topic from the cycle — it is the cycle, made audible by a lesion.
